warnings: AIA.NZ is mid-way through a once-in-a-generation, debt-funded capex supercycle (domestic jet terminal + airfield expansion, guided NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr capex through the end of the decade, targeted completion ~2029). Reported FCF has been negative every year FY2023-FY2025 (-NZ$247m to -NZ$581m) and is projected to remain deeply negative through roughly FY2030 in this model before turning strongly positive as the capex program tapers to a maintenance level. A rigorous WACC-based DCF that discounts this full negative-then-positive path produces a materially lower intrinsic value than the market price, because Gordon-growth terminal capitalization at a textbook 7-8.5% WACC cannot replicate the ~24.6x EV/EBITDAFI multiple the market currently pays for this regulated monopoly asset (a duration/scarcity premium typical of listed airport infrastructure). This gap is a genuine and important finding, not a modeling error -- it is consistent with the qualitative risk factors already flagged (actual aeronautical returns of 5.53% vs a 7.82% regulatory target, and a recent consensus price-target cut from NZ$9.00 to NZ$8.25). Treat the DCF intrinsic values below as a conservative cash-flow-based floor, and cross-check against the EV/EBITDAFI memo figure and peer/regulatory-asset-base valuation approaches before concluding the stock is overvalued.

SBC is immaterial for AIA.NZ (share-based payments reserve balance of only NZ$2.2m at FY2025, an annual expense of roughly NZ$0.3-0.5m via a small executive long-term incentive share-rights plan covering 8 people) and does not meaningfully affect the valuation or share count.

inputs.sbc_source: FY2025 10-K Note 19(c) share-based payments reserve (balance NZ$2.2m FY2025 vs NZ$1.9m FY2024); immaterial LTI share-rights plan for 8 executives
inputs.note_on_last_fcf: last_fcf is Year-1 (FY2026) OWNER FCF from the component build (revenue x EBITDAFI margin - SBC - D&A, tax-effected, less capex, plus/minus working capital), NOT reported trailing FY2025 FCF, because reported FCF is deeply negative during the capex supercycle and not representative of a 'base' cash flow to grow off. See projections.base.fcf for the full 10-year path.

historical_growth.notes: Reported FCF has been negative every year FY2023-FY2025 (~-NZ$247m to -NZ$581m) due to a once-in-a-generation capex supercycle (domestic jet terminal + airfield expansion, ~NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr through decade-end vs historical maintenance capex of ~NZ$150-260m). FCF-based CAGRs are not meaningful and are omitted; growth driver for the DCF is revenue (aeronautical volume/price recovery + property rent-roll growth), with owner FCF built from EBITDAFI margin, D&A, tax, capex-guidance and working-capital components rather than extrapolated from history. Equity CAGR is distorted by the Sep-2024 NZ$1.4bn placement/retail equity raise (shares 1472m->1688m) and is not used as the primary growth driver.

base.rationale: Revenue growth decelerates from post-recovery/near-term fuel-shock-affected ~5% (FY26) toward a long-run ~4% (passenger + inflation) by FY35, with a mid-decade bump (FY28-29) as new domestic jet terminal capacity is commissioned. EBITDAFI margin ramps from 69.8% (FY25 actual) toward 73% (mature, PSE5 regulatory reset support). Capex follows management's own guidance of NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr 'until the end of the decade', peaking ~FY28 as the domestic jet terminal completes (~2029 per Master Plan), then tapering to a ~NZ$320m/yr (~19% of revenue) maintenance level. Cash tax rate held at 27% (close to FY25 effective 24.1% and H1-26 effective 27.5%, near NZ's 28% statutory rate -- no abnormal one-off to ramp away).

bull.rationale: Faster international passenger recovery above 2019 levels, successful new route wins (e.g. China Eastern), PSE5 regulatory settings modestly more favourable post the WACC merits-review litigation, and continued property rent-roll outperformance (Manawa Bay, Landing Business Park).

bear.rationale: 2026 Middle East fuel-price shock and airline capacity cuts (Air NZ, Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) persist longer than expected, PSE4/PSE5 regulatory settings stay unfavourable (actual returns keep lagging the 7.82% target), capex program runs over budget/schedule, and higher-for-longer interest rates raise funding costs on the ~NZ$2.65bn+ debt pile.

bear.note: A negative equity intrinsic value in the bear case is a genuine model output, not an error: it reflects that the ~NZ$1.0-1.6bn/yr capex program is largely already committed/contractual (NZ$1.31bn of PP&E purchase obligations at Dec-2025) and debt-funded, so a scenario combining sustained capacity cuts, weaker margins, and a higher WACC leaves owner FCF unable to service the resulting debt build without either delaying capex, cutting the dividend, or raising further equity. Read as a warning signal (leverage/refinancing risk in a severe downside), not a literal negative per-share value.

cross_check_memo.description: Market-implied EV/EBITDAFI multiple cross-check (NOT the primary valuation method). AIA.NZ's regulated-monopoly infrastructure profile trades at a duration/scarcity premium that a textbook WACC-based Gordon-growth DCF does not capture.
cross_check_memo.note: For reference, applying the current ~24.6x EV/EBITDAFI multiple to Year-10 base-case EBITDAFI (NZ$1,252m) implies an EV of roughly NZ$30.8bn -- multiples of the DCF-derived enterprise value. This illustrates the gap between a cash-flow-discipline valuation and observed market pricing for this asset class; it is not itself a recommended fair-value estimate.

base.note: Because interim FCF (Years 1-8) is deeply negative during the capex supercycle, even the fair-value-consistent 15%-IRR entry price is at or below zero on this model -- i.e. no price today compensates a buyer at a 15% hurdle for absorbing 8 years of cash-negative capex investment ahead of the payoff, at these WACC/terminal-growth settings. This is a direct consequence of the capex trough and should be read alongside the cross-check memo, not in isolation.

sensitivity.note: Sensitivity built off the BASE-case FCF path (10yr). Rows = WACC (5.5%-9.5%), Columns = terminal growth (1.25%-3.25%). Low-WACC rows are flat because the 20x FCF terminal cap binds rather than Gordon growth.

sanity_check.basis: SBC-adjusted on both sides (AIA SBC is immaterial, NZ$0.1-0.6m/yr, so adjusted ~= GAAP; these deliberately differ from screener P/E which uses GAAP EPS). Historical multiples use June FY-end closing prices. Outlier years excluded from averages: FY2018 & FY2021 (investment-property revaluation gains inflate earnings), FY2020-FY2023 (COVID border closure and recovery distortion), FY2024 (NZ$5.5m NPAT from the one-off deferred-tax charge after NZ removed building depreciation deductions) - kept in the table for visibility.
sanity_check.note: Check passed in the over-valuation direction it is designed to catch, but the gap runs the OPPOSITE way: base IV NZ$1.90 implies ~6.7x EV/EBITDA vs a 15.7-19.6x historical trading range. The market persistently pays a duration/scarcity premium for monopoly airport infrastructure that a 7.5% WACC Gordon-growth DCF discounting 5-8 years of negative capex-supercycle FCF cannot reproduce. See cross_check_memo and warnings: the DCF says AIA is expensive relative to owner cash flows, not that the model tripped.
